newsitem.title: USA: UAW workers strike Chrysler engine plant.
newsitem.headline: UAW workers strike Chrysler engine plant.

text.p: About 1,800 workers at Chrysler Corp Mound Road engine plant went on strike early Thursday over outsourcing issues in a dispute that could curtail production of some of the company's highly profitable truck models.

Members of United Auto Workers Local 51 walked off their jobs after a midnight EST deadline expired. Negotiations aimed at ending the strike and reaching an agreement for a new local labor contract were expected to resume by mid-morning Thursday, said Chrysler spokesman Tony Cervone said.

Most of the engines built at Mound Road are used in Chrysler's Dodge Ram and Dakota pickup trucks. They include a 3.9-liter V-6, the 5.2-liter and 5.9-liter V-8s and a monster 8-liter V-10 used in the heaviest versions of the Ram.
The 5.2-liter V8 also is a popular option in the Jeep Grand Cherokee sport utility vehicle.
A prolonged strike would force Chrysler to shut down production of the nearby Dodge City assembly plant, which produces the Ram and Dakota.
Cervone declined to speculate on how long it would take for engine shortages to start.

Union officials plant said the dispute centers on Chrysler's plans to shift production of driveshafts from the plant to outside suppliers, a move that would eliminate up to 300 jobs from the factory's payroll.
The strike comes hours after Chrysler announced plans for new investments of $1.3 billion in six Detroit manufacturing plants, which did not include the Mound Road engine plant.

Chrysler had previously planned to close the plant after it launched production of a new generation of engines next year at the Mack Avenue engine plant in Detroit, which is now undergoing a $900 million renovation, which includes new investments of $150 million announced Wednesday.
Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said Wednesday that the Mound Road plant could be kept open depending on the outcome of negotiations with the UAW.

Meanwhile, a strike by UAW Local 1999 strike at General Motors Corp.'s Oklahoma City car assembly plant entered its sixth day early Thursday. Union and company negotiators are still said to be far apart in the dispute over staffing levels at the plant.

The union has demanded that GM add 500 jobs to the plant's payroll to help replace workers lost to retirements and transfers. GM is defending recent moves to shrink the plant's workforce as necessary to make it competitive.
